patient.chief_complaint: Sudden brief loss of consciousness while standing in his kitchen, witnessed by a neighbor
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Robert Caldwell is a 67-year-old Caucasian male with a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes (diet-controlled), and hyperlipidemia who presents to the emergency department by ambulance after a single episode of transient loss of consciousness. His neighbor, who had stopped by for a visit, reports that the patient was standing at his kitchen counter when he suddenly collapsed without any prodromal warning, falling forward and catching himself partially on the countertop. He was unresponsive for an estimated 10 to 15 seconds, then regained consciousness spontaneously and immediately asked what had happened. There was no convulsive activity, no tonic stiffening, no rhythmic jerking, no tongue biting, and no urinary incontinence. Recovery was described as immediate and complete — he was coherent and conversational within 30 seconds. The neighbor noted that just before the event the patient had commented he felt his heart 'racing' for a few seconds. He endorses approximately three months of episodic palpitations that he describes as a rapid fluttering sensation in his chest, generally lasting 10 to 30 minutes and resolving on their own. His primary care physician evaluated him for these episodes eight weeks ago. An ECG performed in the office at that visit showed a rate of 88 bpm with a regular rhythm and was documented as 'sinus rhythm, normal.' He was reassured that the palpitations were likely related to anxiety given an ongoing stressful period following retirement, and no further workup was arranged at that time. He has not been started on any new medications. He denies chest pain, dyspnea at rest, exertional pre-syncope, fever, recent illness, or ingestion of stimulants or new supplements. He has had no prior syncopal episodes. On review of systems, he endorses fatigue for the past two to three months and mild exertional dyspnea when climbing stairs, which he attributed to deconditioning.

results.title: 2018 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope
results.finding: Supraventricular tachycardia, including atrial flutter with rapid ventricular response, is a recognized cause of arrhythmic cardiac syncope. ECG documentation of the arrhythmia at the time of or preceding syncope establishes the diagnosis.

results.title: 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the evaluation and management of patients with syncope
results.journal: Journal of the American College of Cardiology
results.finding: Cardiac monitoring to capture symptom-rhythm correlation is recommended in patients with syncope and suspected arrhythmic etiology. Inpatient telemetry is appropriate for high-risk presentations.

results.title: Cavotricuspid isthmus ablation for typical atrial flutter: efficacy and guideline support
results.authors: Per ACC/AHA/HRS 2019 focused update on catheter ablation of cardiac arrhythmias
results.journal: Journal of the American College of Cardiology
results.finding: Catheter ablation of the cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI) is the preferred long-term rhythm-control strategy for typical (counterclockwise, type I) atrial flutter with acute procedural success exceeding 95%. Rate control with AV-nodal agents is appropriate for immediate ventricular rate management.

results.title: Anticoagulation in atrial flutter: CHA2DS2-VASc risk stratification
results.authors: Per AHA/ACC/HRS 2019 focused update on atrial fibrillation
results.journal: Journal of the American College of Cardiology
results.finding: Patients with atrial flutter carry a thromboembolic risk comparable to atrial fibrillation. CHA2DS2-VASc score guides anticoagulation decisions; score of 2 or greater in males is generally an indication for long-term anticoagulation. Anticoagulation is also required if cardioversion is planned.

output.summary: Atrial flutter with rapid ventricular response is an established cause of arrhythmic cardiac syncope, particularly during episodes of 1:1 AV conduction. ESC 2018 and ACC/AHA/HRS 2017 guidelines support ECG documentation and cardiac monitoring as the primary diagnostic tools. Cavotricuspid isthmus ablation is the preferred definitive therapy for typical atrial flutter. Anticoagulation is guided by CHA2DS2-VASc scoring, with identical risk stratification to atrial fibrillation.

output.proposed: Metoprolol succinate (rate control, AV-nodal agent) and Apixaban (anticoagulation) in a patient on Lisinopril, Hydrochlorothiazide, and Atorvastatin
interactions: Metoprolol + Hydrochlorothiazide: additive antihypertensive effect; monitor blood pressure and heart rate during titration.
Apixaban + Atorvastatin: no clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction at standard doses; both are CYP3A4/P-gp substrates but combination is generally well tolerated at standard dosing.
contraindications: Concurrent use of a beta-blocker and a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (verapamil, diltiazem) for rate control: risk of symptomatic bradycardia, high-degree AV block, and hemodynamic compromise — avoid combination without specialist oversight.
Digoxin combined with additional AV-nodal agents: additive risk of bradycardia and high-degree AV block during flutter; monitor closely if combination used.
NSAIDs or aspirin combined with apixaban without a compelling indication: additive bleeding risk.
warnings: If cardioversion is planned: anticoagulation must be therapeutic for at least 3 weeks prior, or transesophageal echocardiogram must be performed to exclude left atrial appendage thrombus, per standard AF/flutter cardioversion protocols.
Monitor potassium and renal function periodically with concurrent HCTZ and lisinopril — electrolyte disturbances can affect atrial conduction.
Lisinopril: monitor for hypotension if additional antihypertensive or rate-control agents are added.
alternatives: Diltiazem (non-DHP CCB): alternative rate-control agent when beta-blocker is contraindicated; do not combine with beta-blocker.
Rivaroxaban or dabigatran: alternative direct oral anticoagulants if apixaban is not tolerated.

critical_actions: Recognise atrial flutter with rapid ventricular response (1:1 conduction) as the arrhythmic cause of syncope based on ECG and telemetry correlation
Initiate continuous inpatient telemetry with defibrillator availability
Start AV-nodal rate-control agent (beta-blocker preferred; do not combine with non-DHP CCB) to control ventricular rate
Initiate anticoagulation after calculating CHA2DS2-VASc score (score 3 in this patient: age 65+, hypertension, diabetes)

Do not combine a beta-blocker and a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker for rate control (risk of high-degree AV block and hemodynamic compromise)

Do not conclude that the prior office ECG documenting 'sinus rhythm, normal' at 88 bpm excludes a significant arrhythmia — a snapshot ECG during 4:1 flutter conduction can mimic a normal rate; paroxysmal 1:1 conduction requires monitoring to detect

key_reasoning_points: Atrial flutter at 2:1 conduction (~150 bpm) can transition abruptly to 1:1 conduction at ~300 bpm when AV-nodal refractoriness is transiently reduced, producing a catastrophic drop in cardiac output sufficient to cause syncope — this mechanism was captured directly on telemetry

The prior office ECG documented as 'sinus rhythm at 88 bpm' almost certainly represented atrial flutter at 4:1 or variable conduction on that snapshot; a single normal-rate ECG does not exclude paroxysmal arrhythmia and should not halt workup when recurrent palpitations are present
TSH must be checked in every new-onset atrial flutter to exclude hyperthyroidism as a reversible precipitant; normal TSH in this case makes hyperthyroidism unlikely
Troponin negativity excludes ACS-related arrhythmia and confirms flutter as a primary rhythm diagnosis
CHA2DS2-VASc score of 3 (age 65+: 1 point, hypertension: 1 point, diabetes: 1 point) mandates anticoagulation — risk in atrial flutter equals atrial fibrillation
Cavotricuspid isthmus ablation is the preferred definitive treatment for typical (counterclockwise, isthmus-dependent) atrial flutter with >95% acute success rates

The current 12-lead ECG and telemetry definitively establish atrial flutter with rapid conduction as the syncopal mechanism.
